items.title: Verification Behavior and Metacognitive Calibration in AI-Assisted Clinical Reasoning Among Physiotherapy Students: Cross-Sectional, 3-Group Comparative Study
items.abstract: Background Generative AI is part of everyday study in the health professions. Safe use is thought to depend less on how much students use it than on how they handle its output: checking it, reasoning soundly when it is wrong, and keeping confidence aligned with accuracy. Which behaviors are associated with better performance is untested in physiotherapy education. Objective We tested (1) whether status in a structured “AI in Healthcare” elective (no course exposure, currently taking, or completed) was associated with performance on a clinical case examination (basic knowledge, case-based reasoning, and hallucination-trap items) and with metacognitive calibration, and (2) among students who used AI during the examination, whether self-reported cross-checking of AI output or the quantity of AI use was associated with performance. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 137 (71%) of the 193 invited physiotherapy students (no course exposure: n=67; currently taking: n=43; completed: n=27) completed a researcher-developed 30-item open-resource examination with item-level confidence ratings and an AI-use survey (cross-check frequency; number of AI-assisted questions). Prespecified primary outcomes were the hallucination-trap score, case-based reasoning, and the calibration gap. The per-participant Brier score was the confirmatory calibration test. Group contrasts used Kruskal-Wallis tests and heteroscedasticity-consistent regression adjusted for age, year, grade point average, and prior AI use. Among 108 AI users, cross-check frequency and AI-use quantity were modeled jointly, then adjusted for demographics, course group, and basic-knowledge score. Results Cross-check frequency was associated with total score (β=2.98, 95% CI 1.27-4.68; P<.001), persisted after adjustment for demographics and course group (β=2.81, 95% CI 1.26-4.36; P<.001) and after excluding fast completions, and attenuated once basic-knowledge score was added (fully adjusted β=1.08, 95% CI –0.09 to 2.24; P=.07). AI-use quantity was not positively associated with performance (β=–0.26, 95% CI –0.53 to 0.00; P=.05). Calibration differed by group on the per-participant Brier score (H2=10.23; P=.006) and expected calibration error (H2=12.31; P=.002), both worst in the completed group (calibration gap: β=0.078, 95% CI 0.023-0.132; P=.005; accuracy at maximum confidence: 70.5%, 95% CI 44.8%-93.2%; 61 responses from 14 participants). Currently taking students outscored no-course-exposure peers on case-based reasoning (β=1.01, 95% CI 0.21-1.81; P=.01) and hallucination-trap items (β=0.92, 95% CI 0.06-1.79; P=.04), but not after excluding 11 completions under 5 minutes; basic knowledge did not differ (P=.74). Conclusions In an open-resource clinical examination, performance was associated with how students verified AI output, not how much they used it. The clearest deficit was metacognitive calibration rather than accuracy. These prespecified associations identify verification behavior and confidence calibration as measurable candidate targets for AI-literacy instruction. Because the design is cross-sectional and verification was self-reported, their instructional value requires testing in randomized or longitudinal designs.

items.title: Workload, social support, and job stress among nurses: A moderation analysis
items.abstract: Background: Job stress is a serious occupational health concern in nursing. High workload is consistently identified as a primary stressor, particularly for inpatient nurses who provide continuous 24-hour care and perform complex clinical and administrative tasks. Theoretically, this dynamic is analyzed through the Buffering Hypothesis, which positions social support as a potential moderating variable to protect individuals from the adverse effects of job stressors. Objective: This study aimed to analyze whether social support serves as a moderating variable in the relationship between workload and job stress among inpatient nurses at RSD dr. Soebandi Jember. Method: This quantitative study with a cross-sectional design was conducted from September 2025 to February 2026. Primary data were collected from 105 staff nurses selected via proportional random sampling from an accessible population of 124 nurses. Workload was measured using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), social support with the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS), and job stress with the Perceived Stress Scale-10 (PSS-10). Data were analyzed using Spearman’s rank correlation and Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA). Results: Most respondents reported a heavy workload (53.3%), high social support (44.8%), and moderate job stress (55.2%). Statistical tests indicated a weak but significant positive relationship between workload and job stress (r = 0.216, p = 0.027). Social support was independently associated with lower job stress (B = -0.552, β = -0.671, p < 0.001), whereas the interaction between workload and social support was not statistically significant (B = 0.007, β = 0.125, p = 0.092). Conclusion: Social support functions as an independent predictor that directly lowers job stress but does not act as a moderating variable in mitigating the impact of heavy workloads. This finding is supported by the Optimal Matching Theory, highlighting a mismatch between available emotional-relational support and structural-operational job demands.

items.title: Workplace Flexibility, Health Status, and Subjective Work Performance: Evidence from Japanese Panel Data
items.abstract: Workplace flexibility may have different implications for work performance depending on its form and workers’ circumstances. Using nationally representative panel data from the Japan Household Panel Survey and Keio Household Panel Survey (JHPS/KHPS), this study examines whether schedule- and location-based flexibility are associated with subjective work performance and whether these associations vary by health status. The baseline analysis uses 7678 person-year observations from 3259 workers aged 20–64 in 2019–2021 and estimates random-effects ordered logit models. Poor self-rated health is consistently associated with lower subjective work performance. Schedule-Based Flexibility (SBF) shows the clearest positive baseline pattern: it is associated with a 10.2 percentage-point increase in the probability of high subjective work performance (SWP ≥ 7) among workers reporting poor health, compared with 2.5 percentage points among those not reporting poor health; the difference in average marginal effects is 7.7 percentage points (p = 0.035). However, the SBF × poor-health interaction turns negative in 2022–2024 and is statistically insignificant in the pooled 2019–2024 analysis, indicating substantial temporal heterogeneity. The remote-work estimates are statistically imprecise. The findings suggest SBF may be relevant to sustainable, health-supportive work design, but warrant cautious, noncausal interpretation.

items.abstract: Мета статті – побудувати модель оцінювання організаційної адаптивності ІТ-команд у кризових умовах. Потребу в моделі зумовлено тим, що адаптивність команди, яку розглядають як ключове джерело стійкості компанії, не має вимірювальної форми. Адаптивність розкладено на чотири складники – структурну, процесну, технологічну і психологічну стійкість. Систему показників побудовано у два шари: інституційний фіксує спостережуваний факт наявності організаційної опори складника, перцептивний – оцінку цього складника учасниками команди. Шкалу рівнів зрілості (реактивний, фрагментарний, керований, відтворюваний) побудовано за правилом найслабшої ланки: рівень визначає мінімальне, а не середнє значення складників. Модель застосовано до масиву авторського опитування фахівців з управління ІТ-проєктами; визначено межі попередньої валідації та напрями подальших досліджень.

items.title: “The journey is more important than the destination.” The agency of adult learners in the age of generative artificial intelligence from a constructivist perspective
items.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) within adult continuing education has been observed to be a major contributing factor in the transformation of the conditions under which adults construct their knowledge and professional competencies. This article presents a critical analysis of the existing subject literature, addressing the issue of adult learners' subjectivity in educational environments saturated with GenAI. The analysis adopts a constructivist understanding of learning as an active process of meaning-making based on experience, iteration, and reflection. A particular emphasis is placed on the pedagogical category of error, interpreted within the framework of constructivist theories. A critical analysis was conducted of how GenAI is used in the learning of adult workers, what opportunities and limitations it presents from a constructivist perspective, and what consequences it has for the learner's agency in the context of Industry 5.0. This analysis was based on selected publications. In conclusion, a set of meta-competencies and didactic recommendations was proposed that may help protect the right to make mistakes and preserve the agency of adult learners in the era of algorithmic optimisation.

items.title: “Why the face?”: Exploring Robot Error Detection Using Instrumented Observer Reactions
items.abstract: How do humans recognize and rectify social missteps? We achieve social competence by looking around at our peers, decoding subtle cues from others around us — a raised eyebrow, a laugh — to evaluate the environment and our actions. Robots, however, struggle to perceive and make use of these nuanced reactions. By employing a novel neck-mounted device that records facial expressions from the chin region, we explore the potential of previously untapped data to capture and interpret human responses to robot error. First, we develop NeckNet-18, a 3D facial reconstruction model to map the reactions captured through the chin camera onto facial points and head motion. We then use these facial responses to develop a robot error detection model which outperforms standard methodologies such as using OpenFace or video data, generalizing well especially for within-participant data. Through this work, we argue for expanding human-in-the-loop robot sensing, fostering more seamless integration of robots into diverse human environments, pushing the boundaries of social cue detection and opening new avenues for adaptable robotics.

items.title: “Yes, It’s more Targeted and Efficient”: Students’ Perceptions and Experiences of LLM-Powered AI Agents in Pre-Interpreting Preparation
items.abstract: This study investigated an innovative LLM-powered AI agent in the training of pre-interpreting preparation technique in an undergraduate interpreting course as a discrete language learning context. Over one month, 19 senior English majors engaged with three context-specific AI agents created via a DeepSeek-to-Doubao workflow to deliver a four-tier practice framework aimed at fostering self-regulated learning. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), open-ended survey items, and structured reflection logs. A mixed-methods evaluation revealed overwhelmingly favorable perceptions, driven by compressed preparation time, targeted and automated extraction of terminology and thematic knowledge, and interactive formative feedback. However, the students encountered distinct challenges, including prompt sensitivity, data hallucinations, and speech-recognition inconsistencies. Ultimately, while AI agents served as effective preparatory coaches, successful integration requires a structured verification pedagogy to train students in critical fact-checking and algorithmic boundary navigation.

items.title: A Confidence-Aware Hierarchical Deep Learning Framework with Explainable AI and Large Language Models for Breast Cancer Histopathology Diagnosis and Reporting
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Breast cancer diagnosis from histopathological images must include accurate categorization, reliable uncertainty assessment, comprehensible evidence, and clinically significant reporting. Although deep learning-based histopathological classification has made significant progress, current methods often rely on single-model representations and do not provide sufficient approaches to manage prediction error and incorporate complementary morphological information across geographic scales. Furthermore, categorization, explainability, and clinical reporting are treated as separate tasks, creating a gap between image-level prediction and workflow-based clinical decision support. Methods: In this study, we propose a Task-Delegation Multi-Agent System (MAS) incorporating a Generalist Perception Agent (GPA), a Specialist Perception Agent (SPA), and a Clinical Reasoning Agent (CRA) to address these limitations. The GPA (BreastCareNet-G) handles routine cases using multi-scale CNN feature fusion, while the SPA (BreastCareNet-S) acts as a ViT-based consultant for complex morphological patterns. Instead of simple linear routing, we introduce a confidence-driven delegation protocol (0.85 threshold) where the GPA autonomously escalates ambiguous cases to the SPA. In scenarios of persistent evidence conflict, where both perception agents fail to meet the confidence threshold, the CRA (an LLM-based agent) intervenes to analyze the discrepancy, generate a structured diagnostic summary, and mandate an immediate human-in-the-loop review. Results: An analysis of the publicly available BreaKHis dataset demonstrated that the GPA autonomously accepted 2365 cases with a 99.79% accuracy. Based on raw forced-classification logits, the combined system correctly predicted 2368/2373 cases. For the 8 escalated cases, the SPA functioned as an unvalidated reporting adjunct, generating secondary ViT-based metadata for the CRA rather than extending automated clinical sensitivity. Conclusions: The proposed MAS framework effectively orchestrates multi-scale feature extraction, confidence-guided delegation, explainable AI, and LLM-assisted conflict resolution into a unified diagnostic workflow, serving as a robust technical proof of concept for enhancing the dependability and clinical safety of AI-assisted breast histopathology analysis.

items.title: A proposed framework of psychological latency in human adaptation to nano enabled drinking water purification systems
items.abstract: Nano-enabled drinking water purification technologies have emerged as effective solutions for removing chemical, microbial, and emerging contaminants, particularly in decentralized and resource-limited settings. While existing research predominantly emphasizes material performance, removal efficiency and environmental safety, limited attention has been given to how prolonged reliance on invisible and automated nano-based systems influences human risk perception and behavior over time. This narrative review aimed to examine the potential psychological and behavioral implications of nano-enabled drinking water purification systems and to propose the concept of psychological latency as a framework for understanding long-term cognitive, emotional and behavioral adaptation to nano-enabled water purification technologies. The review concentrates on the purification of drinking water through nanotechnology. However, the psychological mechanisms discussed, such as cognitive offloading, trust transfer, reduced vigilance, and over-reliance, are not distinctive to this technology and may also occur in other automated purification systems. Drawing on environmental risk perception, human–technology interaction, and behavioral adaptation frameworks, this review synthesizes evidence suggesting that trust formation, perceived control and vigilance may represent important mechanisms underlying user experiences with nano-enabled water technologies. The synthesis further highlights potential benefits, including anxiety reduction and behavioral normalization, while also highlighting potential concerns such as over-reliance and risk compensation. By integrating psychological dimensions with material and system-level considerations, this review emphasizes the importance of human-centered design features such as transparency, feedback mechanisms, and risk communication. The findings position psychological risk perception as a critical but underexplored component of responsible nano-enabled water purification deployment and provide a foundation for future empirical research, public health policy development and sustainable water intervention design.

items.title: A systematic literature review of work-related stress assessment in industrial experimental studies toward human-centric Industry 5.0
items.abstract: Work-related stress is a growing challenge in the transition toward Industry 4.0 and 5.0, where digitalization, automation, and human–machine collaboration heighten cognitive and mental demands. This review systematically examines recent studies aimed at assessing work-related stress in both real and simulated industrial environments, with a particular focus on mental stress and cognitive workload. This systematic review provides a holistic view of assessment of work-related stress, and it synthesizes current knowledge, identifies gaps and outlines future research directions to help assess, prevent and mitigate work-related stress in next-generation human-centric industrial systems.

items.abstract: Triangulation is widely endorsed in qualitative research, yet its operational logic is often under-specified in single-case studies of classroom engagement, particularly where two course types are compared within one institution. This paper presents a triangulation design for integrating non-participant classroom observation, semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions in a single-case study of student classroom engagement in a resource-constrained higher vocational college in western China. The design is grounded in constructivism and adopts an intrinsic single-case logic in which institutional conditions are held constant while cultural-foundation and practical-training courses operate as contextual lenses for analysing behavioural, cognitive and affective engagement. Three data sources are treated as functionally complementary rather than parallel: observation records observable behavioural phenomena, interviews interpret participants’ cognitive and motivational accounts, and focus groups capture collective perspectives and divergences. The paper specifies a cross-source coding matrix, procedures for confirming consistent evidence and interpreting contradictory evidence, and a thematic chain linking instructional behaviours, perceived classroom environment, intrinsic motivation and multidimensional engagement. items.title: Accountable Delegation: Why Organizations Need Agent-Aware Endpoint Control for AI Agents
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly delegate work to AI agents that run on employees' computers, where they read and change files, execute programs and contact external services, while employees paste business and personal data into AI chat services. Operating systems, identity systems and network controls authorize all of this as the employee, because they know no principal smaller than the user. Data protection law, the EU AI Act, sector regulation and the NIST frameworks nonetheless hold the organization accountable for what its AI does, and they call for least privilege, human oversight, the ability to intervene, and records that withstand scrutiny. From these sources we derive six requirements for governing agents on endpoints. We prove that no control deciding by account, role, device or program can enforce a policy that treats an agent differently from its user, whereas attribution along the chain of processes suffices; that the workload of human oversight is bounded by the number of distinct situations, with the probability that the next request needs a person below $K/(en)$ after $n$ requests; and that rarity of unsafe behaviour offers no protection at organizational scale. After assessing the established control families, we present IOArx, which names the agent behind each file operation, decides it by a policy written for agents, holds the agent while a person decides, gates network connections, inspects submissions to AI services and keeps a hash-chained record, all on the device. In measurements, IOArx attributed processes to their agents without a misattribution, held a violating agent on Linux within a median of 3.1~ms, and raised no false alarm on 32{,}771 real prompts.

items.title: Adaptive Pacing in Human-AI Interaction:
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for writing, retrieval, explanation, planning, tutoring, decision support, and agentic work. Yet much everyday AI use still begins with a familiar interaction pattern: a person enters a prompt, the model generates an answer, and the user reformulates the next prompt. That pattern is useful, but it should not be mistaken for the full design space of personalized human–AI interaction. This white paper proposes adaptive pacing as a technically meaningful layer of AI use. Adaptive pacing concerns how an AI-mediated interaction regulates informational depth, response timing, complexity, progression, and cognitive demand in relation to the user and the task. The proposal moves personalization beyond surface-level response styling toward interaction regulation across an evolving exchange. This trajectory is consistent with emerging research. NIST frames human–AI tasks around human goals and outcomes rather than AI techniques alone [1]. A 2026 survey of personalized LLM-powered agents organizes personalization across profile modeling, memory, planning, and action execution, emphasizing that personalization can permeate the decision pipeline rather than remain confined to response generation [2]. Recent HCI work has also begun testing adaptive token pacing, cognition-aware interventions, and cognitive-load-sensitive interfaces [3–5]. The result is an emerging technical foundation for treating pacing and interaction demand as first-class elements of personalized AI. The paper develops a public conceptual model for Adaptive Interaction Regulation (AIR): Observe → Estimate → Regulate → Respond → Correct → Update. AIR is presented as a research abstraction, not an implementation blueprint. Proprietary pP inference rules, thresholds, memory weighting, orchestration, and cross-component integration remain deliberately unspecified.

items.title: Adoption of Chatbot Technology for Chronic Disease Self-Management: Behavioral Intention of Patients in the Saudi Healthcare Context
items.abstract: Chronic disease self-management requires continuous engagement with symptoms, medications, health information, and lifestyle decisions, creating a need for accessible technologies that can provide ongoing patient support. Despite the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots in healthcare, limited evidence explains their acceptance among patients with chronic diseases. Drawing on an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this study examined how perceived ease of use (PEU), perceived usefulness (PU), perceived information quality (PIQ), and perceived customization (PC) shape patients' behavioral intention (BI) to use chatbots for chronic disease self-management in Saudi Arabia. A quantitative survey was conducted among 305 patients with chronic diseases recruited through convenience sampling via online channels. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed in SPSS with descriptive statistics and simple linear regression. The findings showed that PEU, PU, PIQ, and PC were all significant positive predictors of BI, with PC emerging as the strongest predictor. These results demonstrate that patients' intention to use healthcare chatbots is shaped not only by conventional technology perceptions of usability and usefulness, but also by the quality and personal relevance of chatbot-delivered support. By extending TAM with informational and personalization-related factors, this study provides context-specific evidence on chatbot acceptance among chronic disease patients in Saudi Arabia. The findings offer some practical guidance for healthcare professionals seeking to design and integrate patient-centered chatbot services that are usable, useful, reliable, and responsive to individual self-management needs

items.title: AI governance through the eyes of users: a large-scale study of online reviews
items.abstract: Purpose With the growing importance of artificial intelligence (AI) governance, numerous high-level frameworks have been articulated by policymakers and expert communities to guide the development and application of AI. While such frameworks offer valuable normative orientation, they may not fully capture the practical concerns of those who interact with AI systems in organizational and operational contexts. This study aims to address that gap by exploring bottom-up, user-centered perspectives on AI governance. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a bottom-up approach to explore how governance-relevant themes are expressed in user discourse. Drawing on over 100,000 user reviews of AI products from G2.com, we apply Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Topic Modeling (BERTopic) to extract latent themes and identify those most semantically related to AI governance. Findings The analysis reveals a wide range of governance-relevant topics spanning technical and non-technical domains. These include concerns across organizational processes, such as planning, coordination, and communication, as well as stages of the AI value chain, including deployment infrastructure, data handling, and analytics. The findings show overlap with institutional AI governance frameworks on issues like privacy and transparency, while surfacing overlooked areas such as project management, strategy development, and customer interaction. Originality/value This paper advances AI governance research by introducing a scalable method for identifying governance-relevant topics using semantic similarity and unsupervised topic modeling. It offers a novel, bottom-up mapping of governance concerns as expressed in user discourse, highlights both alignments and blind spots in existing frameworks, and demonstrates how bottom-up user perspectives complement existing AI governance frameworks by revealing governance dimensions that are salient in practice.

items.abstract: An autonomous AI agent may be correctly authenticated, operate inside a secure sandbox, possess legitimate credentials and receive human approval, yet still execute an unintended or unauthorized consequential operation. Conventional AI safety mechanisms address model behaviour, computational isolation and access permissions, but do not necessarily determine whether the exact operation about to occur should become externally effective. This disclosure presents a protected execution architecture based on the fundamental principle that computation is not authority to act. The proposed architecture intercepts consequential operations as Candidate Acts and maintains them in a Non-Effective State. A Protected Enforcement Domain independently validates the actual operation against authorized purpose, destination, execution scope, runtime context, policy state, freshness, revocation and delegation constraints. Protected Validation Evidence is committed before, or atomically with, the availability of a scoped, non-bearer execution capability. A designated Finality Sink independently verifies the capability against the actual pending operation before permitting its consequential effect. items.title: AI Systems Psychology (Part II): Agency Debt as a Measurement Framework for the Erosion of Human Agency under routine AI exposure
items.abstract: Every AI system in production is measured but the people who rely on it aren’t. Routinely handing a mental task to a machine weakens the ability behind it, while the output keeps looking fine. We propose a measure for that loss. Agency Debt is the cumulative shortfall in the six AI-IARA agency preserving capacities (Awareness, Interpretation, Intention, Action, Relational agency and Autonomy) across an exposed population, measured at intervals against what each person could do before the system arrived. It joins a tradition of counting hidden losses (e.g. sleep and technical debt to frailty and poverty measures). We specify it as a formative construct, derive three quantities a deployment should report, read each as a trajectory through change models, and demonstrate them in two workplace cases. We set out how the measure could mislead, what would refute it, and what must be validated before regulators can rely on it.

items.title: AI-Assisted English Language Learning in Engineering Education: A Review of Emerging Tools, Practices and Employability Outcomes
items.abstract: Engineering graduates continue to face significant employability challenges despite possessing strong technical competencies, largely due to deficiencies in grammatical literacy and professional communication skills. The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence in education offers transformative opportunities to address the above-mentioned gaps. This paper presents a systematic review of the literature examining AI- assisted tools, including Automated Writing Evaluation systems, Large Language Models and career readiness platforms and their capacity to improve grammatical accuracy and employability among engineering students. The review identifies three interrelated frameworks: Constructivist Learning Theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge and Self-Regulated Learning Theory. Findings suggest that AI tools significantly enhance accuracy, communication confidence and learner autonomy when implemented within a teacher-facilitated framework. Similarly, challenges including digital equity, academic integrity and over reliance on automation requires careful attention. The paper concludes with evidence- based recommendations for embedding AI tools within engineering curricula for employment-ready graduates equipped for a rapidly evolving knowledge economy.

items.title: AI-Generated Visual Evidence in Food-Delivery Complaints: Exploratory Consumer Perceptions and Implications for Sustainable Platform Governance
items.abstract: Generative AI creates uncertainty when images are submitted as evidence in food-delivery complaints. This exploratory cross-sectional survey of 314 adults recruited in Romania examines familiarity with AI-generated imagery, perceived manipulation risk, detection confidence, attitudes toward extra verification, and anticipated consequences for trust and honest complainants. Of the 314 respondents, 214 (68.2%) rated manipulation as easy or very easy, whereas 201 (64.0%) considered substituting an AI-generated or external image for a missing genuine photograph unacceptable or rather unacceptable. For additional evidence requests, 225 of 310 respondents selecting a predefined response (72.6%) chose either a reasonable anti-abuse measure or a sign of professionalism; four open-text answers were excluded from this binary classification. Among four prespecified association tests, none remained significant after Holm correction in the full sample. The AI-familiarity–manipulability association was stronger in the exploratory delivery-use-experienced subgroup (n = 272; Spearman’s rho = 0.189; Holm-adjusted p = 0.007). These findings document specific, non-representative consumer opinions rather than observed fraud, procedural fairness, or verification effectiveness. The implications for proportionate platform governance and sustainability remain conceptual and require experimental and operational evaluation.

items.title: AI-Powered Business Intelligence and Advanced Decision Analytics for Improving Enterprise Performance and Digital Competitiveness in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Saudi enterprises are spending heavily on dashboards, data platforms and artificial intelligence (AI), yet the link between these investments and measurable performance is often assumed rather than demonstrated. This review asks how AI-powered business intelligence and advanced decision analytics create enterprise value, which conditions govern that value in Saudi organisations, and how managers can steer analytics investment towards digital competitiveness. A systematic integrative review was conducted of 30 peer-reviewed journal studies published between 2020 and 2025. It was anchored by a survey of business analytics experts in Saudi firms that examined innovation capabilities as a mediator, and by a study of AI capability, data-driven culture and firm performance. Eleven of the 30 studies report evidence from the Kingdom. Three findings stand out. First, analytics and AI improve performance mainly through better and faster decisions, organisational learning and innovation, rather than through technology alone, and data-driven culture and employee analytics skills repeatedly act as the transmission belt. Second, Saudi evidence shows that organisational factors, management support, security and human capital matter more for adoption and performance than infrastructure per se, while recent panel studies associate AI and digital transformation with stronger environmental, social and governance results among listed firms. Third, the appropriate division of labour between managers and algorithms depends on how structured and uncertain a decision is. The paper proposes a decision-value framework that links capability resources, decision modes, performance outcomes and competitiveness, together with a matrix for allocating decisions between automation, augmentation and human judgement, and an agenda for research in the Kingdom.

items.title: Algorithmic benevolence or responsibility coercion? How AI-generated content information types shape green purchase intention
items.abstract: Whether Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) subtly promotes green consumption or triggers consumer resistance remains theoretically underexplored. Drawing on responsibility internalization theory and psychological reactance theory, this study conducted three online studies to examine the mechanisms through which AIGC information types (evidence-oriented vs. value-oriented) influence consumers’ green purchase intention. The results indicate that value-oriented information generates higher green purchase intentions than evidence-oriented information, while simultaneously eliciting stronger responsibility internalization and perceptions of autonomy threat. Further analysis reveals that power distance belief (PDB) plays a significant moderating role in the relationship between information types and two psychological responses. Additionally, perceived consumer effectiveness (PCE) moderates the outcomes of these dual psychological mechanisms; high PCE not only reinforces the positive impact of responsibility internalization on green purchase intentions but also, to some extent, mitigates the resistance effect triggered by autonomy threats. This study reveals the “double-edged sword” effect of generative AI (GAI) in green marketing, offering valuable practical guidance for enterprises to optimize GAI communication strategies and enhance green marketing effectiveness.

items.title: An empirically evaluated online classroom framework for enhancing 21st-century competencies in higher education: a mixed-methods study
items.abstract: Introduction This study develops and empirically evaluates an online classroom framework designed to support 21st-century competencies in higher education by integrating connectivism and social constructivism within a digital humanism paradigm. Addressing the limitations of passive, lecture-based virtual classrooms, the proposed framework incorporates retrieval-augmented artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, real-time collaborative whiteboards, hierarchical mastery learning paths, and micro-credential digital badges to scaffold critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, and digital literacy. Methods Employing a four-phase exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, the study began with a contextual needs analysis involving 250 undergraduate students and 40 lecturers at a public university in Thailand, followed by system prototyping, expert design adequacy validation (n = 3), and a 16-week semester classroom pilot across two undergraduate database courses with two instructors and 100 students. Results In Phase 1, thematic analysis of qualitative reflections and multiple regression modeling indicated that online classroom environment structure (β = .421, p < .001), active learning activities (β = .385, p < .001), and technological support (β = .224, p < .001) significantly predicted perceived 21st-century competency support (R ² = .659, Adjusted R ² = .655, F(3, 286) = 184.24, p < .001, with consistent patterns across student and lecturer subsamples). In Phase 3, the web-based learning management system prototype achieved high expert adequacy ratings (22-item mean M = 4.64, SD = 0.34; domain-average mean M = 4.66). During the Phase 4 pilot, instructors reported high usability satisfaction (M = 4.95, SD = 0.07), and students reported favorable system usability (M = 4.29, SD = 0.52) alongside significant pre- to post-module quiz gains (54.2% to 78.4% on un-gated first attempts, d z = 1.99, p < .001; 84.6% on mastery-gated attempts, d z = 2.42) and behavioral telemetry engagement, supported by qualitative interview excerpts highlighting reduced learning anxiety and Socratic inquiry. Post-implementation multiple regression analysis indicated that nine learner experience predictors accounted for 86.01% of the variance in perceived content understanding (R ² = .8601, Adjusted R ² = .8461, F (9, 90) = 61.474, p < .001; process predictors alone R ² = .7351), with perceived academic achievement (β = .299), knowledge retention and application (β = .284), peer interaction (β = .231), and learning motivation (β = .149) emerging as significant positive predictors, while unscripted collaborative problem-solving exhibited a negative suppression weight (β = -.145, p = .017). Discussion The negative suppression pattern in unscripted group problem-solving may plausibly reflect collaborative cognitive load, coordination friction, or compensatory help-seeking. Overall, these findings offer an empirically grounded blueprint for transitioning higher education online courses into active learning ecosystems.

items.title: An ethical leadership framework for governing responsible artificial intelligence adoption in education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming education by supporting personalized learning, data-informed decision-making, operational efficiency, and access to educational resources. However, its adoption raises ethical concerns involving algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital inequity, transparency, accountability, and professional autonomy. Although guidelines establish principles for responsible AI use, they provide limited direction on translating these principles into educational leadership responsibilities and governance practices. This article addresses this gap by proposing an Ethical Leadership Framework for responsible AI adoption in education. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of literature, international policy documents, and ethics and governance models, the framework identifies four interconnected leadership responsibilities: Ethical Awareness, Risk Management, Responsible Opportunity Realization, and Continuous Reflection. It distinguishes institutional or administrative leadership, responsible for policy direction, procurement, resource allocation, risk oversight, data governance, and accountability, from classroom or instructional leadership, which guides pedagogically appropriate and ethical AI use, verifies outputs, adapts assessment, and monitors learning effects. The two levels are connected through stakeholder engagement, institutional guidance, classroom-based evidence, and reciprocal feedback. The framework positions AI adoption as a shared but differentiated leadership responsibility. Although empirical validation is needed, it offers a grounded basis for research, policy development, and practice toward responsible, equitable, transparent, and sustainable AI implementation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Human Resource Agility Through Digital HR Capabilities
items.abstract: Although the AI adoption for human resource management can support responsive management, its organisational value is partly dependent on the capabilities that it can bring through digital information in day-to-day decisions. This study aims to investigate the relationships between artificial intelligence adoption, human resource agility, and explore the mediating relationships between these factors and determine the effects of artificial intelligence adoption on human resource agility. The sample includes 390 HR eligible respondents in a three-construct partial least squares (PLS) structural equation model (SEM) and five indicators per construct. The results of the measurement assessment indicate that the indicators of the measurement have good reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The direct association between Artificial Intelligence adoption and human resource agility is positive (standardised coefficient 0.220) as is the relationship between Artificial Intelligence adoption and digital HR capabilities (standardised coefficient 0.420). The coefficient value of digital HR capabilities is 0.451 and positive, this means that digital HR capabilities are correlated with human resource agility. The specific indirect effect is 0.189 (95th confidence interval = 0.142, 0.242), which supports complementary partial mediation. The model explains 17.6 per cent of the variance in digital HR capabilities and 33.5 per cent in human resource agility. Small differences between the partial least squares and linear benchmarks were found in the individual indicators when using predictive comparisons. The findings place digital HR capabilities as a concrete path towards organisational responsiveness and adopting AI. The adoption of AI for HR should be paired with manager's skills, accurate employee information, data analytics understanding and digital platform coordination.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and alterity: towards a technopersonalism of professional responsibility of computer engineers
items.abstract: In the current development of artificial intelligence, algorithms tend to take precedence over people in the professional environments where they are designed and applied, which poses a risk of dehumanization that must be addressed through professional responsibility of computers engineers. It is therefore necessary to rediscover a genuine understanding of the person and their bodily and relational dimensions, which will help us understand that authentic interpersonal relationships are based on agapic love—a love that cares for the other by establishing a bond of communion, the foundation of true community. From this perspective, the technocratic model must be replaced by a new vision of technology grounded in the face of the other (technopersonalism), which contributes to the development of AI with a human face and translates into concrete criteria of professional responsibility for those who design, manage, and use AI systems. To this end, we suggest some—though never sufficient—proposals.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Possible Transformation of Psychopathology: Amplification, Modification, or Novelty?
items.abstract: Introduction: Technological environments have long shaped the phenomenology of mental distress by reorganizing perception, cognition, and social interaction. Artificial intelligence (AI) — through recommender systems, conversational agents, and synthetic media — represents an intensified form of such influence, whose pervasive, personalized character may produce subtle yet cumulative effects on mental health. We argue that, rather than generating new diagnostic categories, AI systems modulate attention, social feedback, and reality-testing in ways that reinforce pre-existing vulnerabilities such as anxiety, depression, compulsive behaviors, paranoia, and dissociative tendencies. Areas covered: We examine the key mechanisms underlying this amplification. Algorithmic recommendation systems create personalized "opinion chambers" that reinforce maladaptive beliefs and emotional patterns. Anthropomorphic interactions with chatbots may foster emotional reliance and avoidance of human relationships, particularly among socially vulnerable individuals, increasing the addiction liability of human–AI engagement. Design features such as sycophantic feedback can further stabilize dysfunctional cognitions. Finally, synthetic media, especially deepfakes, erode trust and heighten uncertainty about reality, intensifying symptoms linked to anxiety, paranoia, and derealization. Expert opinion: These mechanisms are best conceptualized not as causes of novel disorders but as transdiagnostic risk factors acting on existing vulnerabilities. We acknowledge that AI-specific symptom constellations may emerge at their intersection; however, such phenomena currently lack empirical validation as distinct clinical entities, and premature reification risks obscuring the underlying mechanisms. Conclusion: The mental health impact of AI is best understood as the outcome of specific, interacting technological features operating as transdiagnostic risk factors rather than discrete diagnostic categories.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Indian Education: Evidence, Challenges, and Future Prospects
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing teaching-learning processes, assessment, educational research, curriculum development and institutional management. Its implications are particularly important in India because of the scale, linguistic and socioeconomic diversity of the education system and the need to prepare learners for a technology-rich society. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 recognises the relevance of emerging technologies, including AI, while also foregrounding equitable access and the development of relevant competencies. This paper presents a conceptual, descriptive and analytical review of policy documents, institutional reports, scholarly literature and selected empirical studies relating to AI in Indian education. It examines applications in personalised learning, intelligent tutoring, assessment, inclusive education, teacher education and research, and analyses institutional evidence from IIT Delhi, IIM Ahmedabad, Aligarh Muslim University and other higher education settings. The review also considers challenges concerning infrastructure, the digital divide, teacher preparedness, academic integrity, privacy and algorithmic bias. Its principal conceptual contribution is a five-pillar, human-centred framework comprising digital accessibility and infrastructure; AI-literate teachers; personalised, accessible and inclusive learning; ethical and responsible governance; and the preservation of human values. The paper argues that AI should complement, rather than replace, teachers’ professional judgement. Because the study is based exclusively on selected secondary sources and is not a systematic review, its institutional examples are illustrative and should not be treated as representative estimates for the Indian education system as a whole. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for equitable, ethical and sustainable AI integration.

items.title: Artificial intelligence capacity in the rural United States: a national qualitative study
items.abstract: Objective To understand how rural hospitals use artificial intelligence (AI) and identify ways to reduce the barriers to safe, effective use of high-quality tools that align with these hospitals’ key priorities. Materials and Methods Stratified random sample drawn from the full population of critical access hospitals (CAHs) in the United States in 2025 (n = 1377) to approximate proportional representation of the 4 census regions. We conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with hospital leadership (eg, CMIOs, CIOs, IT leads) tasked with decision-making about technology. Interviews were conducted between October 20, 2025, and January 23, 2026. Results Drawn from the full population of CAHs in the US in 2025, 256 hospitals were sampled and interviews were completed for a total of 50 CAHs represented by 73 interview participants. Generative AI applications were more common and seen as more valuable for CAH contexts than traditional predictive AI. Primary barriers included infrastructure limitations, cost, and lack of transparency on how AI tools worked. Discussion Despite a desire to implement robust governance, most CAHs did not have the ability to do so and reported a critical need for information, tools, and policies to build their AI governance capacity. Information (peer learning, information from non-commercial sources), tools (registries, model cards), and policy to support technical capacity were perceived as the most responsive ways to build capacity. Conclusion To reduce structural barriers to safe and effective AI decision-making, resources and investment should focus on information sharing with and across rural organizations, AI governance support, and transparency efforts. This will support CAHs in judiciously leveraging available resources and prevent waste on low-quality or misaligned AI tools.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
items.abstract: Introduction and Definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare refers to computational systems that help with analyzing, interpreting, and applying health data in clinical practice, public health practice, research, and administration. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines AI as "the capability of algorithms integrated into systems and tools to learn from data". Early clinical decision support systems, such as MYCIN in the 1970s, demonstrated how computers could be helpful in medical reasoning.Body: Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, multimodal models, and generative AI all fall under AI in healthcare. Image interpretation, clinical documentation, risk prediction, triage, drug discovery, patient monitoring, public health surveillance, and personalized treatment plans represent some of the applications of artificial intelligence in the field. For the technology to be clinically effective, it must be validated, incorporated into clinical workflows, and shown to produce meaningful outcomes. FDA-authorized AI-enabled medical devices are becoming more common in clinical practice, particularly in imaging specialties. Multimodal biomedical AI, foundation models, and large language models that could process text, images, laboratory results, and other health data are the focus of current research. AI tools undergoing research, devices authorized for clinical use, and technologies demonstrated to improve patient outcomes represent distinct stages of development and evaluation.Conclusion: Artificial intelligence may improve healthcare efficiency, clinical decision support, research productivity, and access to care. However, clinical benefits depend on rigorous evaluation and appropriate implementation. Potential risks include algorithmic bias, patient privacy concerns, unreliable outputs, and limited transparency. Human oversight and continued monitoring remain important for responsible implementation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Nuclear Medicine: Ethical and Legal Issues
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in nuclear medicine for image reconstruction, quantification, automated segmentation, radiomics, clinical decision support, and theranostic dosimetry. As AI systems move closer to patient management, ethical concerns involving privacy, informed consent, secondary data use, algorithmic bias, generalizability, explainability, automation bias, professional accountability, and health equity become central. This ethics-focused review briefly summarizes major clinical applications of AI in nuclear medicine and discusses data ethics, fairness, transparency, human oversight, clinical validation, and lifecycle governance. In Türkiye, Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data, guidance from the Personal Data Protection Authority, the Council of Higher Education’s ethical guide on generative AI, and, depending on intended purpose, the Medical Device Regulation constitute the principal framework. Generative AI may support education and research, but hallucination, fabricated references, privacy, and academic-integrity risks require expert verification. Trustworthy AI in nuclear medicine should therefore rely on representative data, task-specific and multicenter validation, transparent subgroup performance, uncertainty communication, human oversight, data security, and continuous performance monitoring.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Science and Physics Education, 2015-2026: An AI-Assisted Bibliometric and Title-and-Abstract Analysis across Fourteen Journals
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) research in science and physics education has expanded rapidly, particularly since the emergence of generative AI. This study maps publication patterns, research characteristics, and citation connections across 14 selected science and physics education journals. OpenAlex searches using fifteen AI-related terms identified 966 unique records published between January 2015 and September 2026. AI-assisted screening retained 333 publications, which were coded using available titles and abstracts. Bibliometric analyses examined publication growth, thematic patterns, and citations within and between the two journal groups. Of the included publications, 87.1% appeared from 2023 onwards. Generative large language models and chatbots accounted for 58.9% of the corpus, while instruction and assessment together represented 48.3% of publications. Among 182 records classified as involving human participants, comparison groups were identifiable in 14.3%, effect sizes in 8.2%, and instrument validity evidence in 5.5%. These frequencies reflect information identifiable in bibliographic records, rather than the absence of these features in the full studies. Laboratory and experimental support was the principal educational function in 27 publications. Citation connections between the journal groups were limited: their reference sets had a Jaccard index of 0.047, and 15.6% of publications cited an included study from the other group. The findings document rapid growth and uneven research emphases within the selected venues. Independent human validation and full-text assessment are needed before drawing firm conclusions about methodological quality or educational effectiveness.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in special education mapping sixty years of research through bibliometric analysis and implications for practice
items.abstract: Despite the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in special education, a comprehensive, longitudinal synthesis of the field’s scholarly evolution remains lacking. This bibliometric review addresses this gap by systematically analysing six decades (1964–2024) of global research, encompassing 977 Scopus-indexed publications. Using VOSviewer for scientific mapping, we investigate publication trends, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns, and international collaboration networks. Our findings reveal a significant acceleration in research output since 2010, although publication activity remains concentrated in high-income countries. Thematic cluster analysis reveals interconnected domains, including machine learning methodologies, assistive technologies, adaptive learning systems, accessibility solutions, and ethical considerations. Citation analyses highlight the field’s strong interdisciplinary roots, demonstrating robust linkages with broader AI and educational technology scholarship. This study offers a descriptive mapping of the intellectual structure and historical development of AI research in special education. Interpretations are confined to observable bibliometric patterns and do not assert pedagogical effectiveness or technological impact. Ultimately, these findings establish an evidence-based foundation for future context-sensitive, pedagogically informed, and ethically grounded research into AI applications in special education. items.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration, Operational Efficiency and Implementation Challenges in Nigerian Deposit Money Banks
items.abstract: This study examined how staff of Nigerian Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) perceive AI-enabled operational efficiency and AI implementation challenges, and whether the two perceptions are related. A crosssectional survey of 438 employees of DMBs was conducted. AI integration was captured through employees' perceptions of AI-enabled operational outcomes rather than through a technical audit of AI deployment. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, one-sample t-tests, simple linear regression, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, Harman's single-factor test and moderated regression. Perceived AI-enabled operational efficiency (M = 3.70, SD = 0.77) and perceived implementation challenges (M = 3.74, SD = 0.80) were both significantly above the scale midpoint (p< .001; d = 0.91 and 0.92), so H1 was rejected. Perceived implementation challenges were positively associated with perceived operational efficiency (â = .404, R² = .163, f² = 0.19, p< .001), so H2 was rejected. This association indicates that respondents who reported more challenges also reported more efficiency; it does not show that challenges improve efficiency. Factor analysis supported discriminant validity (Fornell-Larcker criterion met; inter-factor r = .50), although confirmatory model fit was weak (CFI = .876, RMSEA = .156) and the reliability of the challenges scale was marginal (á = .659; CR = .71). Harman's test (44.0% of variance) did not indicate a single dominant method factor but cannot rule out common method variance. The association did not differ by job role but was weaker among staff with 0-5 years of experience (simple slope = 0.24) than among those with six or more years (simple slope = 0.57). Because the data are selfreported, single-source, cross-sectional and drawn from a non-stratified sample, the findings describe staff perceptions in the sampled banks and do not establish causation or actual bank-level performance. The study shows that perceived efficiency gains and perceived implementation constraints co-occur among Nigerian bank staff and supports structured, tenure-sensitive AI training.

items.abstract: This article examines the ontology of artificial intelligence development, its essence, principles of construction, and areas of application, as well as its future prospects. Artificial intelligence is defined as an intelligent robot or a machine trained by humans to perform specific functions. Its primary areas of application include tasks that are dangerous to humans, activities where human physical or mental energy is expended inefficiently, and processes that do not require human creativity or inspiration.

items.title: Balancing Benefit and Sacrifice: A Dual-Path TAM-VAM Integration to Explain Students' Intention to Use Gemini AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: While generative AI reshapes higher education, understanding the psychological trade-offs that drive students' digital use remains critical. Because the Intention-to-Use items in this study ask about continuing to use Gemini AI throughout one’s studies rather than about a first-time adoption decision, the construct is best understood as a continuance-oriented usage intention rather than an initial-adoption intention. This study integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Value-based Adoption Model (VAM) to examine how perceived benefits and sacrifices relate to students’ attitudes, perceived value, and ultimate intention to use Gemini AI. Using a quantitative survey approach, data from 248 university students in East Java who had experience with Gemini AI in academic tasks were analysed using PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4. The structural model explained 54.5% of the variance in Intention to Use (R² = .545), 41.9% in Attitude (R² = .419), and 37.3% in Perceived Value (R² = .373). Perceived Benefit was significantly and positively associated with both Attitude (β = .638, p < .001) and Perceived Value (β = .602, p < .001), whereas Perceived Sacrifice showed a smaller but statistically significant negative association with both constructs (β = −.115 and −.113, p < .05). Both Perceived Value and Attitude, in turn, significantly and positively predicted Intention to Use (β = .348 and .451, p < .001), with a larger coefficient for Attitude. Bootstrapped indirect effects were all significant (via Attitude and Perceived Value, respectively: β = .288 and .209 for Perceived Benefit; β = −.052 and −.039 for Perceived Sacrifice), with the attitudinal route carrying a somewhat larger share. Theoretically, this research synthesizes value and cognitive-affective pathways, offering a holistic framework for Gemini AI usage intention that jointly captures calculative cost–benefit evaluation and affective attitude formation, thereby extending single-pathway adoption models. To our knowledge, this is among the first tests of an integrated dual-path VAM–TAM model for a generative, conversational AI tool in an emerging higher-education market, clarifying the relative weight of value-based versus attitudinal routes. In practice, the findings suggest that AI developers and educators must actively minimize user sacrifices while maximizing the functional academic utility to foster sustainable digital usage in university ecosystems. The findings further highlight that sustainable AI adoption requires not only perceived usefulness but also institutional support, ethical guidance, and student AI literacy.

items.title: BEYOND AUTOMATED FEEDBACK: DEVELOPING CRITICAL THINKING, CREATIVITY, AND COMMUNICATION THROUGH AI-SUPPORTED ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING
items.abstract: This study explores how artificial intelligence can be integrated into English language teaching to foster students’ critical thinking, creativity, and authentic communication skills. In the context of digital transformation, it examines the potential of AI-powered tools to reinforce grammatical knowledge, expand vocabulary, improve speaking and writing proficiency, and address individual learning needs of students. Simultaneously, this study considers the pedagogical challenges associated with excessive reliance on AI, particularly its potential implications for independent thinking, creative problem-solving, and learners’ readiness for authentic communication. A human-centered approach is proposed, emphasizing the integration of AI tools with teacher guidance, independent analysis, collaborative learning and reflective practice. This article argues that the educational value of AI should be assessed not merely by its capacity to automate language-related tasks but also by its contribution to meaningful language development and learner autonomy. This approach seeks to support the development of independent, creative, and communicatively competent English language learners while ensuring that technological innovation remains aligned with fundamental educational goals.

items.title: Beyond heart rate: Beat-to-beat ECG morphology for trust-related state classification
items.abstract: Trust is a fundamental construct in human–automation interaction (HAI), yet electrocardiogram (ECG)-based trust sensing remains limited by inconsistent findings and narrow feature representations. This study compares heart rate variability (HRV), which primarily characterises inter-beat timing, with beat-to-beat (B2B) ECG features that retain additional waveform-level timing and amplitude information for trust-related state classification. ECG signals were recorded from 13 participants during a controlled word- and scenario-cued trust/distrust elicitation paradigm. Across HRV representations, within-participant discrimination was higher than cross-participant discrimination for some feature sets, indicating representation-dependent limitations in cross-participant transfer in the present sample. Under the primary cross-participant evaluation, B2B significantly outperformed the combined time- and frequency-domain HRV representation (HRV-Full; AUC = 0.649 versus 0.453; exact paired p = 0.0059 ). However, its advantage over the strongest HRV-only representation, frequency-domain HRV (HRV-FD; AUC = 0.561), was not statistically significant ( p = 0.1086 ). Importantly, although B2B showed nominal evidence of above-chance cross-participant discrimination (raw p = 0.0155 ), this result did not survive false discovery rate (FDR) correction across the four unique predictive representations ( q = 0.0620 ). Nevertheless, the comparative advantage of B2B over HRV-Full persisted under zero-shot evaluation (AUC = 0.643 versus 0.493; exact paired p = 0.0144 ), indicating that this finding did not depend on participant-specific calibration. To further interpret the B2B representation, fold-wise SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified repeatedly selected model-attributed features related to PR-interval and waveform-amplitude variability. Taken together, B2B features provided greater cross-participant discrimination than HRV-Full in this exploratory sample, while substantial inter-participant variability, lack of FDR-corrected above-chance B2B performance, and modest absolute generalisation highlight the need for larger-scale validation in interactive HAI settings.

items.title: Beyond human-in-the-loop: governing AI agents through the authorship of justification
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) agents in organizations challenge a basic premise of decision governance, that keeping humans in the loop is sufficient to preserve meaningful control. AI agents increasingly frame problems, filter information, generate alternatives and produce the rationales that make recommendations appear reasonable, so humans may remain formally accountable while losing influence over how decisions are formed and justified. The central governance challenge is shifting from controlling autonomous actions to governing algorithmically mediated judgment. Design/methodology/approach This is a viewpoint article. The argument is conceptual, developed through a single running vignette, a manager approving an AI-generated workforce-reduction plan, with analogical anchors from safety engineering and clinical practice and foundations in the behavioral theory of decision-making and institutional theory. The vignette is a stylized composite. Findings Human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop and human-in-command locate control in a person's formal position leave open whether that person can reconstruct, challenge or alter the justification behind a decision. Each can therefore collapse into ratification, passive supervision and nominal authority. The paper develops epistemic governance to preserve human authorship of organizational justification. It specifies three enabling conditions (reconstructability, contestability, role separation), calibrates oversight intensity to irreversibility and answerability and introduces epistemic audits of organizational judgment rather than algorithmic output. Originality/value This viewpoint relocates the AI governance debate from decision loops to the authorship of justification, treating the reasoning behind a decision and the purpose it serves as two faces of one act of authorship and offers a practical mechanism (the epistemic audit) for testing whether human authorship is present before consequential decisions are approved.

items.title: Beyond the PhD: Agentic Research Orchestration and the Democratization of Scholarly Authority
items.abstract: Generative AI and multi-agent systems can now assist with literature discovery, hypothesis generation, code execution, and manuscript preparation, yet academic recognition remains organized around institutions, degrees, authorship conventions, and publication channels. This paper asks whether human direction of AI research teams can constitute a scholarly contribution eligible for independent recognition, introduces agentic research orchestration (ARO) as a proposed research practice, compares seven primary research-integrity, contributorship and assessment instruments, and proposes a six-domain assessment rubric, integrity safeguards, a public research dossier and a falsifiable pilot design. The framework is proposed, not validated; no new empirical results are claimed.

items.title: Beyond Traditional Healthcare IT Consulting: Most Valuable AI Advice Is Knowing When Not to Use It
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from pilots into routine clinical and operational work, healthcare’s most important question is no longer where can AI be used? but where should it not be used? This Viewpoint argues that the decisive capability is not technical adoption but advisory judgment: knowing when AI can improve care, when workflows must be redesigned, and when the risks outweigh the benefits. Evidence from AI adoption, clinical documentation, model validation, and governance shows that AI creates value only when use cases are clearly defined, workflows are redesigned, performance is locally validated, and accountability for errors is explicit. Even promising applications, such as ambient documentation, remain imperfect and require ongoing clinician oversight. Implications for medicine: AI should be treated as a clinical and organizational intervention, not merely an IT deployment. Physicians and healthcare leaders must retain responsibility for validation, workflow integration, patient safety, and professional judgment. Before adoption, organizations should require advisors to make the case against an AI project; those that survive this scrutiny are more likely to deliver safe, measurable, and trustworthy improvements in care.

items.title: Beyond Traditional Teaching: Exploring Teachers' Perceptions and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
items.abstract: This study investigated teachers’ beliefs, attitudes, awareness, and perceived challenges regarding the utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and learning at higher education institutions in Multan District, Pakistan. A descriptive quantitative survey design was employed. Data were collected through an online, self-structured questionnaire comprising 45 statements organized into three domains: awareness of AI tools, perceived impact on teaching effectiveness, student engagement and assessment, and challenges associated with AI use. Although the thesis reports that 290 faculty members were selected, 163 completed questionnaires (67 male and 96 female) were included in the reported analysis. Frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations were used for descriptive analysis, while independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA were used to examine group differences. Overall, respondents expressed favorable perceptions of AI and its potential contribution to routine academic tasks, lesson preparation, personalized learning, instructional methods, assessment design, and feedback. Lack of training, insufficient technological infrastructure, limited institutional support, ethical concerns, data privacy, and academic dishonesty were identified as important barriers. Department-based differences were statistically significant across all three perception domains. Gender differences were significant for awareness and perceived impact but not for challenges; no significant differences were reported by teaching sector, teaching experience, academic qualification, or academic position. The study concludes that meaningful AI integration requires teacher development, institutional support, adequate infrastructure, and clear ethical and academic policies. As the data represent teachers’ perceptions, the findings should not be interpreted as direct evidence of improved student achievement.

items.title: Bias, Persepsi Keadilan, dan Strategi Mitigasi pada Rekrutmen Berbasis Kecerdasan Buatan: Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in recruitment, yet evidence on its bias, perceived fairness, and mitigation strategies remains scattered across disciplines. This study aims to map and synthesize empirical literature on fairness in AI-based recruitment within business and management. A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, using the Scopus database with a search string covering technology, recruitment context, and fairness issues for publications from 2021 to 2026. Of 237 records retrieved, 166 English-language journal articles were screened, and 30 empirical studies were analyzed through narrative and thematic synthesis. The results show that 16 of the 30 studies were published in 2025–2026. Experiments, simulation and computational studies, and surveys were the most frequent designs, with the United States, Germany, and China as the dominant contexts. Gender bias was the most frequently reported form (11 studies), followed by racial bias (three studies), while disability and age bias were rarely examined. Applicants tended to view algorithmic evaluations as less fair than human evaluations, and these perceptions were shaped by prior discrimination experiences and system transparency. Fifteen studies reported mitigation strategies, grouped into technical improvements, transparency and explanation, and governance; the most direct evidence came from debiasing word representations and modifying interview questions. These findings indicate that reducing measurable bias does not always lead to applicant acceptance, so fairness in AI-based recruitment should be examined at two levels: outcome fairness and perceived fairness in the selection process.

items.abstract: This article provides a theoretical and methodological analysis of reflective and axiological mechanisms underlying the formation of professional and deontological competence in future specialists, examining their psychological characteristics and potential improvement within higher education. Particular attention is paid to the interrelationships among awareness of professional duty, internalization of moral values, independent evaluation of one's actions, responsible decision-making, and reflective analysis of the consequences of professional activity. The theoretical foundations of psychological factors contributing to professional and deontological competence are discussed, including value orientations, professional identity, moral reflection, empathy, intrinsic motivation, and self-regulation. The article examines how integrating reflective and axiological approaches can support the development of students' professional and ethical positions, conscious acceptance of professional values, and ability to make ethically justified decisions in complex professional situations. Based on an analysis of scientific literature, an integrative mechanism is proposed, comprising value-motivational, reflective-cognitive, emotional-moral, and behavioral-regulatory components. The methodological potential of reflective journals, ethical dilemma analysis, professional scenario modeling, mentoring, and activities aimed at increasing awareness of personal values is also explored. The proposed approach is intended to strengthen future specialists' professional responsibility and improve the theoretical and methodological foundations of their ethical and professional preparation.

items.title: Career Adaptability, Perceived Usefulness of Generative AI, and Innovative Work Behavior: The Conditional Role of Occupational Future Time Perspective and Psychological Safety
items.abstract: Employees differ in whether they use generative artificial intelligence (AI) in new ways. Drawing on career construction theory, we ask whether occupational future time perspective (OFTP), usually treated as a resource, favors engagement with it regardless of psychological safety, and whether career adaptability relates to innovative work behavior through usefulness appraisals. We tested these questions with a two-wave survey of 525 employees in South Korea, adjusting each outcome for its baseline. OFTP was negatively associated with perceived usefulness under low psychological safety and nearly unrelated under high safety, so its indirect association with innovative work behavior was negative under low safety. Career adaptability was associated with innovative work behavior through perceived usefulness, although perceived ease of use shared this mediating role. The moderation depended on concurrent measurement of safety and was reproduced by job autonomy, so we treat it as tentative. An expansive occupational future does not uniformly favor AI engagement: where employees do not feel safe to experiment, it goes with less favorable appraisals. Building career adaptability alongside a climate that tolerates experimentation may support innovative work behavior.
